title: Ulceration Care: Preventing, Treating, and Healing Foot Ulcers
author: Alex M. Stewart, DPM, FACFAS
excerpt: Foot ulceration is a serious medical condition that requires timely and specialized care. Without proper treatment, foot ulcers can lead to infection, chronic foot…
body: Foot ulceration is a serious medical condition that requires timely and specialized care. Without proper treatment, foot ulcers can lead to infection, chronic foot pain, and potentially limb-threatening complications. At Advanced Foot & Ankle Specialists of Arizona, we provide comprehensive ulceration care for patients in Chandler, Arizona, as well as nearby communities such as Gilbert, Mesa, and Tempe, with a focus on healing, prevention, and long-term foot health.

A foot ulcer is an open wound that commonly develops on the bottom of the foot, toes, or around the ankle. Ulcers form when prolonged pressure, friction, or injury causes the skin to break down. Because the feet are weight-bearing, these wounds can be slow to heal without professional care. Ulceration is especially common in individuals with diabetes, poor circulation, nerve damage, or structural foot deformities, though anyone experiencing chronic foot pain, ill-fitting footwear, or trauma can be affected.

Several risk factors increase the likelihood of developing a foot ulcer, including diabetic neuropathy, peripheral arterial disease, bunions, hammertoes, calluses, limited mobility, and a history of previous ulcers. Reduced sensation in the feet can prevent patients from noticing cuts or pressure points, allowing wounds to worsen over time. This makes early evaluation by a podiatrist critical to avoiding complications.

Symptoms that should never be ignored include an open sore that does not heal, redness or swelling around the wound, drainage or foul odor, thickened callused skin with breakdown underneath, increasing foot pain, or signs of infection such as warmth or fever. Early ulceration care significantly improves healing outcomes and reduces the risk of hospitalization or surgical intervention.

Research shows that most lower-extremity amputations are preceded by a foot ulcer that was not treated early. With appropriate wound care, pressure relief, and medical management, many ulcers can heal successfully. Early intervention helps reduce infection risk, accelerate healing, preserve mobility, and protect overall health.

At Advanced Foot & Ankle Specialists of Arizona, Alex Stewart, DPM, FACFAS and Antonius Su, DPM provide individualized ulceration care using advanced diagnostic and treatment options. Our services include thorough foot evaluations, X-ray and ultrasound imaging, professional wound care and debridement, infection management, MLS Laser Therapy to promote tissue healing, foot and ankle therapy, protective offloading techniques, custom orthotics, and surgical care when necessary. Our approach focuses not only on healing the ulcer but also on correcting the underlying cause to prevent recurrence.

Preventing future foot ulcers is an essential part of long-term care, particularly for patients with diabetes or circulation issues. Daily foot inspections, proper hygiene, supportive footwear, avoiding barefoot walking, managing blood sugar levels, and scheduling routine podiatric visits all play a vital role in prevention. Patients with a history of ulceration benefit greatly from ongoing monitoring and preventive care.

If you are experiencing a non-healing wound, increasing foot pain, or signs of infection, prompt treatment is essential. Early ulceration care can mean the difference between successful healing and serious complications. title: Platelet-Rich Plasma (PRP) for Heel and Ankle Pain: Benefits, Process & Results
author: Alex M. Stewart, DPM, FACFAS
excerpt: If you’re dealing with persistent foot or ankle pain that isn’t improving with rest, stretching, physical therapy, or anti-inflammatories, you may be wondering if…
body: If you’re dealing with persistent foot or ankle pain that isn’t improving with rest, stretching, physical therapy, or anti-inflammatories, you may be wondering if there are more advanced options available. One of the most exciting treatments we offer at Advanced Foot & Ankle Specialists of Arizona is Platelet-Rich Plasma (PRP) therapy.

PRP has become increasingly popular in sports medicine and orthopedic care because it uses your body’s own healing potential to support recovery—especially for chronic tendon and ligament injuries. At our office, we commonly see patients from surrounding communities who have pain that has lingered for months and are looking for a non-surgical solution.
In this blog, I’ll explain what PRP is, when it works best, and how we determine whether it’s the right treatment plan for you.
What Is Platelet-Rich Plasma (PRP) Therapy?
Platelet-Rich Plasma (PRP) is a regenerative medicine treatment that uses a concentrated portion of your own blood to promote tissue healing.
Here’s the key concept: platelets are not only responsible for clotting—they also contain powerful growth factors and healing proteins that support tissue repair. In PRP therapy:

1. A small amount of blood is drawn (similar to routine lab work).
  2. The blood is placed into a centrifuge to separate the components.
  3. The platelet-rich portion is concentrated.
  4. PRP is injected into the injured or inflamed tissue.
Because PRP is derived from your own body, it is generally considered very safe and well-tolerated.
Why PRP Is Different from Traditional Injections
Many patients are familiar with steroid injections, but PRP is very different.

• Steroid injections may reduce inflammation quickly, but they do not rebuild damaged tissue.
  • PRP is designed to stimulate healing in tissues with poor blood supply (like tendons and ligaments), which is why chronic injuries often respond well.
At Advanced Foot & Ankle Specialists of Arizona, PRP is often considered when conservative therapy hasn’t fully resolved a problem—or when we want to avoid surgery when appropriate.
What Conditions Can PRP Help Treat?
PRP is most effective when pain is caused by chronic inflammation or tissue degeneration, particularly tendon-related conditions.
Some common conditions we treat with PRP include:
Plantar Fasciitis
If you experience heel pain, especially with the first steps in the morning, you may have plantar fasciitis. PRP can help reduce inflammation and promote healing of the plantar fascia.
Achilles Tendonitis
Achilles tendonitis is common in runners, active adults, and “weekend warriors.” PRP can support tendon recovery by stimulating repair in chronically irritated tissue.
Ankle Sprains / Chronic Ligament Pain
Repeated ankle sprains can lead to instability and chronic pain. PRP may help support ligament healing, especially when paired with bracing and physical therapy.
Tendinitis
PRP can also help treat:

• Peroneal tendonitis
  • Posterior tibial tendonitis (common in flat feet)
  • Any other chronic tendon injuries affecting foot or ankle
Arthritis (Certain Cases)
PRP may provide symptom relief for some types of arthritis in the foot and ankle by reducing inflammation. While it does not “cure” arthritis, it may help improve comfort and function.
How PRP Works (What’s Happening Inside Your Body)
After PRP is injected, platelets release growth factors that trigger a healing response. This can:

• Reduce inflammation over time
  • Encourage new tissue repair
  • Improve tendon structure
  • Support long-term recovery
It’s important to know that PRP is not like a numbing injection. It doesn’t typically provide immediate relief. PRP works gradually as tissue remodeling occurs.
What to Expect During PRP Treatment
PRP is performed in-office and usually takes 30 minutes.
Your PRP visit typically includes:

• Evaluation and diagnosis
  • Imaging as needed (X-ray and/or ultrasound)
  • Blood draw
  • PRP preparation
  • Injection into the affected area
Ultrasound-Guided PRP Injections
When appropriate, we use ultrasound imaging to guide PRP injections. This helps ensure the PRP is placed precisely where it needs to go—especially for tendon injuries and areas with complex anatomy.
This is a major advantage and supports better accuracy and outcomes.
Recovery After PRP: Downtime and Timeline
Most patients can resume light activities within 1–2 days, but full recovery varies.
Common post-treatment expectations:

• Mild to moderate soreness for several days (this is normal)
  • Avoid high-impact activity temporarily (running/jumping)
  • Gradual return to activity based on improvement and exam findings
  • Healing response may take several weeks
  • Some cases benefit from a series of PRP injections
We often recommend pairing PRP with supportive care such as:

• Custom orthotics
  • Bracing
  • Foot and ankle therapy (physical therapy)
  • Shoe modifications and activity guidance
Is PRP Right for You?
PRP can be an excellent option if:

• You’ve had symptoms for weeks to months
  • Conservative care has helped but not fully resolved the issue
  • You want a treatment option that supports healing
  • You prefer to avoid surgery if possible
  • You are healthy enough to undergo the procedure
PRP may not be recommended if you have:

• Active infection
  • Certain blood disorders
  • Severe medical instability
  • Some medication restrictions (we review this with you)
The best way to know is through a proper medical evaluation.
Our Approach at Advanced Foot & Ankle Specialists of Arizona
At Advanced Foot & Ankle Specialists of Arizona, our focus is not just treating pain—it’s identifying the cause.
When someone comes in with foot pain or ankle pain, our goal is to build a plan that fits your lifestyle and long-term mobility goals. That may include:

• Diagnostic imaging (X-ray and ultrasound)
  • MLS Laser Therapy
  • Conservative treatments like taping, stretching, bracing
  • Custom orthotics
  • PRP for appropriate cases
  • Surgical planning if needed
Schedule a PRP Consultation in Chandler, Arizona
If you’re struggling with chronic heel pain, tendonitis, ankle pain, or lingering injuries—and you’re wondering if PRP may help—don’t wait.

title: Neuropathy Treatment: Relieving Nerve Pain and Protecting Foot Health
author: Alex M. Stewart, DPM, FACFAS
excerpt: Neuropathy is a common condition that affects the nerves and often causes foot pain, numbness, tingling, or burning sensations in the feet and ankles. These symptoms…
body: Neuropathy is a common condition that affects the nerves and often causes foot pain, numbness, tingling, or burning sensations in the feet and ankles. These symptoms can interfere with walking, balance, and daily activities, especially when left untreated. At Advanced Foot & Ankle Specialists of Arizona, we provide comprehensive neuropathy treatment for patients in Chandler, Arizona, and nearby communities including Gilbert, Mesa, and Tempe, with a focus on symptom relief, prevention of complications, and long-term foot health.

Peripheral neuropathy occurs when nerves that carry signals between the brain, spinal cord, and the rest of the body become damaged. In the feet and ankles, this nerve damage can disrupt normal sensation and muscle function. Neuropathy is most commonly associated with diabetes, but it can also result from poor circulation, repetitive injuries, vitamin deficiencies, infections, certain medications, or nerve compression. Because the feet are farthest from the central nervous system, neuropathy symptoms often appear there first and may gradually worsen over time.

Common symptoms of foot and ankle neuropathy include burning or tingling sensations, numbness, sharp or shooting pain, muscle weakness, cramping, or a pins-and-needles feeling. Some patients experience extreme sensitivity to touch, while others lose the ability to feel temperature or pain altogether. This loss of sensation is particularly concerning because it increases the risk of unnoticed cuts, blisters, or pressure points that can lead to wounds or infections, especially in patients with diabetes.

Several risk factors increase the likelihood of developing neuropathy. Diabetes remains the most common cause, but patients with circulation problems, prior injuries, chronic foot pain, or foot deformities may also be at risk. Neuropathy often occurs alongside other podiatric conditions treated at our practice, including plantar fasciitis, tendinitis, ingrown toenails, and diabetic foot complications. Early identification allows for more effective management and reduces the risk of long-term nerve damage.

Early neuropathy treatment is essential because nerve damage can progress if left unaddressed. As symptoms worsen, patients may experience balance problems, difficulty walking, and an increased risk of falls. Advanced neuropathy can also contribute to skin breakdown, ulcers, and infections that heal slowly. Early intervention helps reduce pain, improve function, and protect mobility and independence.

At Advanced Foot & Ankle Specialists of Arizona, Alex Stewart, DPM, FACFAS and Antonius Su, DPM take a personalized approach to neuropathy treatment, beginning with a thorough evaluation to identify the underlying cause of symptoms. Diagnostic tools such as X-ray and ultrasound imaging may be used to rule out structural problems or nerve compression contributing to foot or ankle pain.

Treatment plans are tailored to each individual and may include both conservative and advanced therapies based on symptom severity and overall health. MLS Laser Therapy is often used to help reduce inflammation, improve circulation, and support nerve healing. Foot and ankle physical therapy can improve strength, balance, and coordination, helping patients feel more stable while walking. For patients with pressure-related pain or instability, custom orthotics are designed to redistribute weight, reduce stress on sensitive nerves, and improve overall foot mechanics.

For patients with moderate to severe neuropathic pain, advanced pain management options may be recommended. Qutenza® (capsaicin 8% patch) is an in-office treatment that targets overactive pain receptors and can provide long-lasting relief from nerve pain, particularly for patients with diabetic peripheral neuropathy. In cases where neuropathy symptoms are chronic and resistant to conservative care, spinal nerve stimulators may be considered. These implantable devices deliver mild electrical impulses that help interrupt pain signals before they reach the brain, offering meaningful relief for select patients. When neuropathy leads to skin breakdown or wounds, specialized wound care is provided to promote healing and prevent infection. In select cases, surgical intervention may be necessary to relieve nerve compression or address structural problems contributing to symptoms.

Preventive care and daily management play an important role in controlling neuropathy. Patients are encouraged to inspect their feet daily, wear supportive and properly fitting shoes, and avoid walking barefoot. Managing underlying conditions such as diabetes is critical, as maintaining healthy blood sugar levels can help slow the progression of nerve damage. Regular podiatric visits allow early detection of changes in sensation, skin integrity, or foot structure before serious complications develop.

If you are experiencing persistent foot pain, numbness, tingling, or balance problems, it is important to seek professional care. Neuropathy symptoms should never be ignored, as they may indicate ongoing nerve damage or another underlying foot and ankle condition. Early evaluation allows for timely treatment and can significantly improve comfort and quality of life.

If nerve-related foot pain or changes in sensation are affecting your daily activities, help is available. title: From Turf Toe to Ankle Sprains: Football Foot & Ankle Injury Guide
author: Alex M. Stewart, DPM, FACFAS
excerpt: Football is one of the most physically demanding sports, requiring explosive speed, sharp cutting, sudden stops, jumping, and frequent high-impact contact. While…
body: Football is one of the most physically demanding sports, requiring explosive speed, sharp cutting, sudden stops, jumping, and frequent high-impact contact. While football injuries often bring to mind concussions or knee problems, foot and ankle injuries are incredibly common—and can quickly sideline players at every level, from youth leagues to high school, college, and the NFL. Because the foot and ankle absorb force with every sprint, tackle, and pivot, they’re especially vulnerable to sprains, fractures, tendon injuries, and overuse conditions. At Advanced Foot & Ankle Specialists of Arizona, our board-certified podiatric surgeons Alex Stewart, DPM, FACFAS and Antonius Su, DPM frequently treat athletes from Chandler, Arizona, and surrounding areas like Gilbert, Mesa, and Tempe who are struggling with foot pain, heel pain, or persistent ankle issues after football practices or games.
Understanding the most common football-related foot and ankle injuries—and knowing when to seek professional care—can prevent long-term problems and help players return to the field safely.
Why Foot and Ankle Injuries Are So Common in Football

Football is a “cutting sport,” meaning players repeatedly shift directions with speed and power. Add in collisions, uneven turf, cleats that grip the ground, and fatigue late in games, and you have the perfect setup for foot and ankle trauma. Injuries can happen from a single impact (acute injury) or develop gradually over time (overuse injury). The most common contributing factors include:

• Sudden pivoting and lateral movement
  • Tackles causing the ankle to roll or twist
  • Landing awkwardly after a jump
  • High repetition from practice drills and conditioning
  • Poor footwear fit or worn-out cleats
  • Limited mobility or weakness in the foot/ankle muscles
If you’re in the Chandler area and dealing with ongoing ankle pain or foot pain after football, a proper diagnosis is essential to avoid playing through an injury that could worsen.
Most Common Football Foot and Ankle Injuries
1) Ankle Sprains (The #1 Football Ankle Injury)

An ankle sprain occurs when the ligaments supporting the ankle stretch or tear—often after the foot rolls inward (inversion sprain). In football, this frequently happens when a player is tackled while the foot is planted or steps on another player’s foot.
Common symptoms include:

• Swelling and bruising
  • Pain along the outside or inside of the ankle
  • Difficulty bearing weight
  • Feeling unstable or “wobbly” on the ankle

Even mild sprains can become chronic if not treated correctly. Players who return too soon are at high risk for repeat sprains and long-term instability. At Advanced Foot & Ankle Specialists of Arizona, we evaluate ankle sprains thoroughly and may recommend X-rays to rule out fractures or hidden injuries. Depending on severity, treatment can include bracing, foot and ankle therapy, and recovery planning to help athletes return safely.
2) High Ankle Sprains (Syndesmotic Sprain)

A high ankle sprain affects the ligaments above the ankle joint that connect the tibia and fibula. These injuries often happen when the foot is planted and the leg rotates—common during tackles or pile-ups.
High ankle sprains typically take longer to heal than standard sprains and may be missed if players assume it’s “just another sprain.”
Signs of a high ankle sprain:

• Pain above the ankle
  • Pain when turning the foot outward
  • Difficulty pushing off or sprinting
  • Pain that lingers for weeks
If you’re searching for ankle sprain treatment in Chandler and symptoms aren’t improving, a podiatric evaluation can make all the difference in recovery time and long-term stability.
3) Turf Toe
Turf toe is a sprain of the ligaments around the big toe joint, caused by hyperextension when pushing off or when the toe bends upward forcefully. It is especially common on artificial turf.
Symptoms include:

• Pain and swelling at the base of the big toe
  • Difficulty running or cutting
  • Pain when pushing off the toe
Without treatment, turf toe can lead to long-term stiffness and chronic foot pain. Treatment may include immobilization, anti-inflammatory care, and sometimes custom support.
4) Stress Fractures and Metatarsal Fractures

Football players place intense repetitive force through the bones of the foot—especially the metatarsals (long bones in the forefoot). Stress fractures develop gradually and may start as a mild ache that worsens over time.
Red flags for stress fractures:

• Pain that increases with activity
  • Swelling on top of the foot
  • Pain that improves with rest but returns quickly

A true fracture can happen from direct impact or awkward planting. X-ray imaging is critical for diagnosis, and early detection helps prevent a small injury from becoming a major season-ending fracture.
5) Achilles Tendinitis

The Achilles tendon connects the calf muscles to the heel bone and plays a huge role in sprinting and explosive movement. Overuse, tight calf muscles, and training overload can lead to Achilles tendinitis.
Symptoms include:

• Pain or stiffness in the back of the heel (worse in the morning)
  • Pain when sprinting or running hills
  • Swelling or tenderness along the tendon

Treatment typically includes activity modification, stretching, strengthening, and in many cases MLS Laser Therapy to reduce inflammation and support healing. Players in Chandler, Gilbert, Mesa, and Tempe often seek care when Achilles pain becomes persistent and starts affecting speed and performance.
6) Plantar Fasciitis (Heel Pain)

Plantar fasciitis is one of the most common causes of heel pain, and football athletes often develop it due to repeated impact and running on stiff surfaces. This condition occurs when the plantar fascia (a thick band of tissue on the bottom of the foot) becomes inflamed.
Symptoms include:

• Sharp heel pain, especially with first steps in the morning
  • Pain after practice or games
  • Tightness in the arch or heel

At Advanced Foot & Ankle Specialists of Arizona, we frequently treat plantar fasciitis using a combination of stretching plans, supportive footwear recommendations, and custom orthotics to reduce strain on the heel.
7) Peroneal Tendon Injuries

The peroneal tendons stabilize the outer ankle and are commonly injured during repetitive cutting or after ankle sprains. These injuries can cause pain on the outside of the foot/ankle and may lead to long-term instability if untreated.
Treatment may include bracing, therapy, and imaging when necessary. In some cases, ongoing pain can indicate tendon tearing that may require advanced care.
How We Diagnose Football Foot and Ankle Injuries

Accurate diagnosis is key—especially because many conditions feel similar in the early stages. At our Chandler office, we evaluate injuries with a full examination and may use advanced diagnostic tools such as:

• X-rays to rule out fractures, joint damage, and bone alignment issues
  • Ultrasound to assess tendon injuries and soft tissue conditions
  • Functional movement evaluation for instability, weakness, and return-to-play readiness
Getting the right diagnosis early can shorten recovery time and reduce the risk of reinjury.
Treatment Options for Football Foot and Ankle Injuries

Football athletes need more than “rest and ice.” The right plan should restore function, prevent reinjury, and get players back to competition safely. Depending on the injury, treatment options at Advanced Foot & Ankle Specialists of Arizona may include:

• MLS Laser Therapy to reduce inflammation and accelerate healing
  • Foot and ankle therapy to rebuild strength, stability, and mobility
  • Foot and ankle taping for added support during return-to-play
  • Custom orthotics to control foot mechanics and reduce stress on injured tissue
  • Wound care for turf burns, blisters, or skin breakdown
  • Surgery when injuries involve fractures, tendon rupture, or chronic instability
  • Ingrown toenail removal for painful nails that worsen with cleats and repeated impact
Every athlete’s timeline and needs are different—especially with youth players, high school athletes trying to finish their season, or adults in weekend leagues.
Prevention Tips for Football Players
Many football foot and ankle injuries are preventable with the right training habits and early attention to symptoms. Helpful prevention strategies include:

• Replace worn cleats and ensure proper sizing
  • Strengthen the ankles with balance drills and resistance training
  • Stretch calves and plantar fascia daily
  • Don’t ignore recurring soreness or swelling
  • Treat ankle sprains fully before returning to play
  • Use orthotics or supportive inserts if recommended
If a player continues practicing through pain, a mild injury can quickly become a serious condition.
When to See a Foot and Ankle Specialist
If foot pain or ankle pain lasts more than a few days, worsens with activity, or causes limping, it’s time to get evaluated. You should seek professional care right away if there is:

• Severe swelling or bruising
  • Inability to bear weight
  • Pain that persists for more than 1–2 weeks
  • Suspected fracture
  • Instability or repeated ankle sprains
Prompt treatment improves outcomes and helps players return safely and confidently.

Football injuries of the foot and ankle should never be ignored—especially when early diagnosis can prevent long-term damage and chronic pain. title: Top 5 Foot & Ankle Sports Injuries | Chandler, AZ Podiatrist
author: Alex M. Stewart, DPM, FACFAS
excerpt: Sports are a great way to stay healthy, active, and strong—but they can also place major stress on the feet and ankles. Whether you are an athlete, runner, or weekend…
body: Sports are a great way to stay healthy, active, and strong—but they can also place major stress on the feet and ankles. Whether you are an athlete, runner, or weekend warrior, sports injuries can happen suddenly or develop gradually from overuse. If left untreated, these conditions can lead to chronic foot pain, ankle pain, and long-term mobility issues.

At Advanced Foot & Ankle Specialists of Arizona, Alex Stewart, DPM, FACFAS and Antonius Su, DPM provide expert care for sports injuries in Chandler, Arizona, as well as nearby cities like Gilbert, Mesa, and Tempe. If you are dealing with pain from an injury, visit www.advancedfootankle.com or call (480) 963-9000.
What are the top 5 foot and ankle sports injuries?
The most common sports-related foot and ankle injuries we see include:

1. Ankle sprains
  2. Achilles tendinitis / Achilles injuries
  3. Plantar fasciitis (heel pain)
  4. Stress fractures
  5. Peroneal tendon injuries
Each condition may present differently, but they all share an important pattern: early treatment reduces healing time and helps prevent chronic problems.
1) What is an ankle sprain?

An ankle sprain occurs when the ligaments supporting the ankle are stretched or torn. This typically happens when the foot rolls inward, injuring the lateral ligaments on the outside of the ankle. Ankle sprains are extremely common in sports that involve cutting, jumping, quick movements, or uneven terrain.
What causes ankle sprains in sports?
Common causes include:

• Sudden twists or falls
  • Jumping and landing incorrectly
  • Quick direction changes
  • Playing on uneven surfaces
What are the symptoms of an ankle sprain?
Symptoms may include:

• Sudden ankle pain after twisting the ankle
  • Swelling and bruising
  • Instability or weakness
  • Pain with walking or standing
  • Reduced range of motion
How is an ankle sprain diagnosed and treated?
At Advanced Foot & Ankle Specialists of Arizona, your podiatrist may recommend:

• X-rays to rule out fractures
  • Ultrasound for ligament or tendon assessment
  • Foot and ankle therapy for strength and stability
  • Foot and ankle immbilization or bracing when appropriate
  • Custom orthotics to reduce instability and prevent re-injury
If you’re experiencing an ankle sprain in Chandler, early treatment can make a major difference and reduce your risk of repeat sprains.
2) What is Achilles tendinitis or an Achilles injury?

The Achilles tendon connects the calf muscles to the heel bone. Achilles tendinitis is an overuse condition caused by repetitive strain, commonly seen in runners, basketball players, and athletes who increase activity too quickly.
What causes Achilles injuries?
Common causes include:

• Increased training intensity or mileage
  • Tight calf muscles
  • Poor footwear support
  • Running hills or sprinting frequently
What are the symptoms of Achilles tendinitis?
Symptoms may include:

• Pain or stiffness in the back of the ankle
  • Heel pain, especially in the morning
  • Tenderness or swelling along the tendon
  • Pain that worsens with activity
How is Achilles tendinitis treated?
Treatment options may include:

• Activity modification and stretching guidance
  • MLS Laser Therapy to reduce inflammation and pain
  • Foot and ankle therapy to improve mobility and strengthen supporting muscles
  • Boot immobilization or Ankle Bracing for better support
  • Custom orthotics to improve alignment and reduce strain
If Achilles pain is ignored, it can lead to tendon degeneration or even rupture—so early evaluation is critical.
3) What is plantar fasciitis?

Plantar fasciitis is one of the most common causes of heel pain in athletes. The plantar fascia is a thick band of tissue that supports the arch of the foot. Overuse or repetitive stress can cause inflammation and microtears, leading to significant discomfort.
What causes plantar fasciitis in athletes?
Risk factors include:

• Running on hard surfaces
  • Tight calves or Achilles tendon
  • Flat feet or high arches
  • Poor footwear support
  • Sudden increase in activity
What are the symptoms of plantar fasciitis?
Symptoms may include:

• Sharp heel pain with the first steps in the morning
  • Pain after running or long periods of standing
  • Arch pain or tightness
  • Pain that improves with movement but returns later
How is plantar fasciitis treated?
Our team may recommend:

• Physical exam and imaging if needed
  • MLS Laser Therapy for inflammation reduction
  • Foot and ankle therapy for stretching and strengthening
  • Supportive shoe recommendations
  • Custom orthotics for long-term arch support and pressure redistribution
If you're searching for heel pain treatment in Chandler, this is one of the most common diagnoses—and one of the most treatable with early care.
4) What is a stress fracture?
A stress fracture is a small crack in the bone caused by repeated impact. Unlike a sudden fracture from trauma, stress fractures develop gradually and worsen over time.
Stress fractures are common in:

• Runners
  • Track and field athletes
  • Basketball players
  • Military and high-impact training participants
What are the symptoms of a stress fracture?
Symptoms may include:

• Pain that gradually worsens with activity
  • Pain that improves with rest
  • Localized swelling
  • Pain when pressing over a specific area
How are stress fractures diagnosed and treated?
Diagnosis may include:

• X-rays (though early stress fractures may not always show)
  • Ultrasound imaging or advanced imaging when needed
Treatment may include:

• Activity restriction and immobilization
    • MLS Laser Therapy for inflammation reduction
• Physical therapy

• Supportive devices to protect the bone
  • Gradual return-to-sport guidance
  • Custom orthotics for long-term arch support and correct biomechanics and prevent recurrence
If you suspect a stress fracture, do not “push through it.” Continuing to train can worsen the injury significantly.
5) What are peroneal tendon injuries?

The peroneal tendons run along the outside of the ankle and help stabilize the foot during movement. These injuries are common in cutting sports, trail running, and individuals with ankle instability.
What causes peroneal tendon injuries?
Causes may include:

• Overuse and repetitive running
  • Repeated ankle sprains
  • Ankle instability
  • High-arched foot structure
What are the symptoms of peroneal tendinitis?
Symptoms may include:

• Pain on the outside of the ankle or foot
  • Swelling behind the ankle bone
  • Pain that worsens with activity
  • Feeling of ankle weakness or instability
How is peroneal tendon injury diagnosed and treated?
Treatment options may include:

• Ultrasound to evaluate tendon injury
  • MLS Laser Therapy for pain and inflammation
  • Foot and ankle therapy to strengthen and stabilize the ankle
  • Bracing or supportive footwear
  • Custom orthotics to improve mechanics and reduce strain
More severe tendon tears or instability may require surgery depending on the extent of injury.
When should I see a foot and ankle specialist for a sports injury?
You should schedule an evaluation if you experience:

• Persistent foot pain or ankle pain
  • Swelling that does not improve
  • Pain that worsens with activity
  • Instability, weakness, or repeated injuries
  • Bruising, numbness, or pain after trauma
Prompt diagnosis and treatment can shorten recovery time and prevent long-term complications.

title: Arthritis in the Feet and Ankles: Symptoms, Causes, and Treatment Options
author: Alex M. Stewart, DPM, FACFAS

body: If you’re experiencing foot pain, ankle pain, swelling, or stiffness, arthritis may be the underlying cause. Arthritis is one of the most common conditions affecting joint health, and it can significantly impact your ability to walk, exercise, and complete everyday activities.

At Advanced Foot & Ankle Specialists of Arizona in Chandler, Arizona, our team provides expert evaluation and treatment for arthritis and other joint conditions affecting the feet and ankles. Alex Stewart, DPM, FACFAS and Antonius Su, DPM diagnose the cause of your symptoms and develop a treatment plan designed to relieve pain and restore mobility. To learn more, visit www.advancedfootankle.com or call (480) 963-9000.
What is arthritis?

Arthritis is a widespread condition that affects an estimated 24% of adults in the United States. The term “arthritis” does not refer to a single condition—it describes a group of disorders that cause joint inflammation, leading to symptoms like pain, swelling, stiffness, and reduced movement.

Although arthritis can occur in any joint, it is particularly disruptive when it affects the feet and ankles. These joints support body weight and absorb impact throughout the day. When arthritis develops in the foot or ankle, it can cause progressive discomfort and limit your ability to stay active.
What are the most common types of arthritis?
Two of the most common forms of arthritis include:

• Osteoarthritis
  • Rheumatoid arthritis
There are also other forms of arthritis that may affect the feet—such as gout, reactive arthritis, and septic arthritis—each with different causes and treatment needs.
What is osteoarthritis?
Osteoarthritis is the most common type of arthritis and is often called “wear-and-tear” arthritis. It develops when the cartilage within a joint gradually breaks down over time.
Cartilage is a firm yet smooth tissue that cushions the ends of bones and allows joints to glide easily. When cartilage wears away, bones can begin rubbing against each other. This can lead to:

• Pain
  • Swelling
  • Stiffness
  • Reduced range of motion
  • Bone spur formation
Osteoarthritis usually develops slowly over time. Many patients notice mild foot or ankle pain at first, which gradually worsens with walking, standing, or exercise.
What causes osteoarthritis?
Osteoarthritis is often linked to long-term joint stress and may be worsened by several risk factors, including:

• Age
  • Obesity
  • Prior injuries (fractures, sprains, ligament injuries)
  • Repetitive stress on the feet and ankles
  • Genetics
  • Foot structure problems or deformities
Osteoarthritis is most common in people over age 50, but younger adults can develop it too—especially if they have a history of sports injuries or repetitive impact activities.
What is rheumatoid arthritis?
Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is an autoimmune disorder. Instead of protecting the body, the immune system mistakenly attacks healthy joint tissue, causing chronic inflammation and progressive damage.

RA can affect joints throughout the body, but it commonly impacts the small joints in the feet, which can cause pain with walking and standing. In some cases, foot and ankle symptoms may be one of the earliest signs of rheumatoid arthritis.
Because rheumatoid arthritis is systemic and inflammatory, it requires early diagnosis and a coordinated treatment plan to reduce long-term joint damage.
Are there other types of arthritis that affect the feet?
Yes. In addition to osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis, other forms of arthritis can affect the feet and ankles, including:

• Gout (often affects the big toe joint with sudden severe pain)
  • Reactive arthritis
  • Septic arthritis (a joint infection that may require urgent treatment)
Because symptoms overlap, an evaluation from a foot and ankle specialist is important for accurate diagnosis.
What are the symptoms of arthritis in the feet and ankles?
Arthritis symptoms can vary based on the type and severity of your condition. Common symptoms include:

• Foot pain or ankle pain
  • Morning stiffness
  • Swelling around the joint
  • Warmth near the joint
  • Tenderness
  • Redness
  • Pain that worsens with activity
  • Decreased range of motion
  • Difficulty walking or standing for long periods
Many patients also change how they walk to avoid discomfort. Over time, compensating for pain may contribute to knee, hip, or back issues.
If these symptoms are affecting your daily life, it is important to schedule an evaluation as soon as possible.
How is arthritis diagnosed?

At Advanced Foot & Ankle Specialists of Arizona, diagnosing arthritis starts with an in-depth evaluation. Alex Stewart, DPM, FACFAS and Antonius Su, DPM will perform a physical exam, review your medical history, and evaluate your symptoms and joint function.
Depending on your condition, diagnostic testing may include:

• X-rays to evaluate joint space narrowing, deformity, and bone spurs
  • Ultrasound imaging to assess soft tissue inflammation and joint changes
  • Blood tests when rheumatoid arthritis or inflammatory arthritis is suspected
If you’d like to schedule a diagnostic evaluation, call: 480-960-9000 or visit our appointment page here: Book an appointment online: https://www.advancedfootankle.com/contact-us
How is arthritis treated?

Arthritis treatment depends on the type of arthritis, severity of symptoms, and how much joint damage is present. The goal is to reduce inflammation, relieve pain, improve mobility, and help patients return to daily activities with less discomfort.
Your personalized treatment plan may include:
Medication
Anti-inflammatory medications may be recommended to reduce pain and swelling. Certain inflammatory arthritis conditions may require additional medication management.
Physical therapy
Foot and ankle therapy can help improve:

• joint range of motion
  • strength and stability
  • walking mechanics
  • mobility and balance
Orthotics

Custom orthotics are one of the most effective non-surgical treatments for foot arthritis. Orthotics can reduce stress on painful joints by improving alignment and redistributing pressure while walking.

Learn more about our orthotic solutions here:
Custom Orthotics
Supportive podiatric care
Footwear guidance, activity modifications, and supportive care can all reduce daily joint strain. Many patients experience meaningful improvement by combining supportive shoes with orthotics.
Surgery (when needed)
In severe cases, arthritis may cause significant pain and loss of function despite conservative care. At that point, surgical options may be considered to restore stability and reduce pain.

If you want to learn more about our surgical approach and services, visit:
Foot & Ankle Services
When should I see a podiatrist for arthritis?
You should schedule an appointment if you have:

• Persistent foot pain or ankle pain
  • Swelling or stiffness that doesn’t improve
  • Difficulty walking
  • Symptoms that worsen over time
  • Sudden severe pain in the foot or big toe (possible gout)
Early treatment helps prevent arthritis from progressing and may reduce the likelihood of long-term joint damage.

title: Foot and Ankle Cancer: Recognizing the Warning Signs and Seeking Early Treatment
author: Alex M. Stewart, DPM, FACFAS
excerpt: Foot and ankle cancer is uncommon, but when it occurs, early detection is critical. Because cancer in the foot or ankle often resembles common conditions such as foot…
body: Foot and ankle cancer is uncommon, but when it occurs, early detection is critical. Because cancer in the foot or ankle often resembles common conditions such as foot pain, ingrown toenails, non-healing wounds, or even ankle sprains, it may go undiagnosed until it becomes more advanced. At Advanced Foot & Ankle Specialists of Arizona, we prioritize early recognition and thorough evaluation for patients in Chandler, Arizona, as well as surrounding areas including Gilbert, Mesa, and Tempe, to ensure serious conditions are identified promptly.

Foot and ankle cancer refers to malignant tumors that develop in the skin, soft tissues, bones, or nail unit of the foot or ankle. These cancers may originate locally or spread from another area of the body. Common types include skin cancers such as melanoma and squamous cell carcinoma, soft tissue sarcomas, bone tumors, and cancers that affect the toenail. Because the feet are subject to daily pressure, friction, and minor trauma, abnormal lesions or wounds are often mistaken for routine podiatric problems, delaying diagnosis.

Symptoms of foot and ankle cancer can be subtle and progress gradually. Warning signs include a wound or ulcer that does not heal, a growing lump or mass, unexplained swelling, changes in skin color or texture, bleeding or drainage from a lesion, dark streaks or discoloration beneath a toenail, or persistent foot pain that does not improve with standard treatment. Any abnormality that continues to worsen or fails to heal should be evaluated by a podiatrist.

A useful screening tool for identifying potentially concerning skin changes is the ABCDE rule for cancer detection, which applies to the feet and ankles as well. A stands for Asymmetry, meaning one half of a lesion does not match the other. B is for Border, referring to irregular, jagged, or poorly defined edges. C is for Color, including uneven coloring or multiple shades such as brown, black, red, white, or blue. D is for Diameter, with lesions larger than a pencil eraser (about 6 millimeters) warranting evaluation, although smaller lesions can still be concerning. E is for Evolving, which refers to any change in size, shape, color, elevation, or symptoms such as bleeding, itching, or pain. Pigment changes beneath a toenail or color spreading beyond the nail should also be assessed promptly.

Several risk factors may increase the likelihood of developing foot and ankle cancer. These include a history of skin cancer, excessive sun exposure, chronic non-healing wounds, repeated trauma or irritation, immune system disorders, and underlying conditions such as diabetes. Patients with diabetic foot issues or poor circulation may be at higher risk for delayed diagnosis, as wounds are more common and healing is often slower.

Early diagnosis significantly improves treatment options and outcomes. When identified in its early stages, foot and ankle cancer can often be treated with localized care and less invasive procedures. Delayed diagnosis may require more extensive surgery and can impact mobility, function, and overall health. If a lesion, wound, or area of foot pain does not respond to appropriate care, further evaluation is essential.

At Advanced Foot & Ankle Specialists of Arizona, Alex Stewart, DPM, FACFAS and Antonius Su, DPM take a comprehensive approach to evaluating suspicious foot and ankle conditions. Diagnostic tools such as detailed physical examinations, X-rays, and ultrasound imaging help assess bone and soft tissue abnormalities. When indicated, patients may be referred for biopsy or additional testing. Treatment options may include wound care, surgical excision of suspicious lesions, corrective surgery, custom orthotics to relieve pressure, foot and ankle therapy, and coordination with oncology specialists when necessary.

Routine foot care and regular podiatric visits play an important role in early detection. Patients should inspect their feet regularly, monitor skin and nail changes closely, wear properly fitting shoes to reduce irritation, and seek medical attention for persistent foot pain or abnormalities. These preventive habits are especially important for individuals with diabetes, circulation problems, or a history of foot ulcers.

If you are experiencing unexplained foot or ankle pain, a non-healing wound, nail discoloration, or a changing skin lesion, do not delay care. While many foot and ankle conditions are benign, ruling out serious causes such as cancer is essential. To schedule an evaluation, contact Advanced Foot & Ankle Specialists of Arizona at (480) 963-9000 or visit www.advancedfootankle.com. Our team proudly serves Chandler and the surrounding East Valley and is committed to protecting your foot and ankle health.

title: Struggling with Ingrown Nails? Learn How to Prevent and Treat Them
author: Alex M. Stewart, DPM, FACFAS
excerpt: At Advanced Foot & Ankle Specialists of Arizona, we understand how painful and frustrating ingrown toenails can be. Whether you’re in Chandler, Mesa, Gilbert, or…
body: At Advanced Foot & Ankle Specialists of Arizona, we understand how painful and frustrating ingrown toenails can be. Whether you’re in Chandler, Mesa, Gilbert, or Tempe, we want to help you prevent and treat this common foot condition that can interfere with your daily activities. Ingrown toenails are a condition where the edge of a toenail grows into the surrounding skin, causing pain, swelling, and sometimes infection.
In this blog, we will walk you through everything you need to know about ingrown toenails, from identifying the symptoms to exploring effective treatments and preventive measures.
What is an Ingrown Toenail?

An ingrown toenail occurs when the edge or corner of a toenail grows into the skin surrounding the nail, leading to pain and inflammation. The condition most commonly affects the big toe, but can occur with any toenail.
Causes and Risk Factors
Several factors can contribute to the development of ingrown toenails, including:

• Improper Nail Cutting: Cutting toenails too short or rounding the edges can increase the likelihood of the nail growing into the skin.

  • Tight or Ill-Fitting Shoes: Shoes that don’t allow enough room for your toes can cause pressure, contributing to the growth of an ingrown toenail.

  • Trauma: A sudden injury to the toe, such as dropping something heavy on it, can cause the nail to grow abnormally and become ingrown.

  • Genetics: Some individuals may inherit a natural predisposition to develop ingrown toenails due to the shape of their nails or feet.

  • Poor Foot Hygiene: Not keeping your feet clean and dry can increase the risk of infection and worsen the condition.

  • Excessive Sweating: The moisture from sweaty feet can soften the skin and make it more vulnerable to toenail penetration.
Symptoms of Ingrown Toenails
Ingrown toenails can present with a variety of symptoms, which may include:

• Pain and Tenderness: You may experience sharp pain around the affected toenail, especially when wearing shoes or walking.

  • Swelling: The area surrounding the toenail may become swollen, making it difficult to wear shoes comfortably.

  • Redness: Inflammation around the nail is often accompanied by redness, indicating irritation or infection.

  • Pus or Drainage: If the ingrown toenail becomes infected, you might notice pus or drainage from the affected area.

  • Difficulty Walking: In severe cases, the pain and swelling may make it difficult to walk or perform daily tasks.
Treatment Options for Ingrown Toenails

Ingrown toenails can usually be treated conservatively, but in some cases, professional care from a podiatrist is necessary. At Advanced Foot & Ankle Specialists of Arizona, we offer a range of treatments for ingrown toenails, depending on the severity of the condition.
1. Conservative Treatments

• Proper Nail Care: Trim the nails straight across and avoid cutting them too short to reduce the risk of the nail growing into the skin.

  • Warm Soaks: Soaking the foot in warm water with Epsom salt can help reduce swelling and pain.

  • Topical Antibiotics: If an infection is present, applying an over-the-counter antibiotic ointment can help prevent it from spreading.

  • Padding and Cushioning: Using cotton or gauze to gently lift the nail can help relieve pressure and reduce discomfort.
2. Medical Interventions
If conservative treatments do not provide relief, our podiatrists, Dr. Alex Stewart, DPM, FACFAS and Dr. Antonius Su, DPM, may recommend more advanced interventions:

• Partial Nail Removal: In cases where the ingrown toenail is persistent, a portion of the nail may be removed to allow the skin to heal.

  • Matrixectomy: In severe cases, a portion of the nail matrix (the root of the nail) may be removed to prevent the nail from growing back into the skin.

  • Surgical Procedure: For recurrent ingrown toenails, a minor surgical procedure may be required to remove the nail or the affected part of the nail.
Preventing Ingrown Toenails
While some factors like genetics can’t be avoided, there are several steps you can take to prevent ingrown toenails from developing:

• Wear Comfortable Shoes: Ensure that your shoes provide enough space for your toes to move freely. Avoid tight or narrow shoes that put pressure on the toes.

  • Proper Foot Hygiene: Keep your feet clean and dry, especially between the toes, to reduce the risk of infection.

  • Trim Your Toenails Correctly: Always cut your nails straight across and avoid rounding the edges. Never cut them too short.

  • Use Foot Care Products: Over-the-counter products like toenail softeners can help prevent ingrown nails, particularly if you’re prone to them.
When Should You See a Podiatrist?

If your ingrown toenail causes persistent pain, swelling, or signs of infection (such as redness or pus), it’s important to seek professional care. At Advanced Foot & Ankle Specialists of Arizona, we are committed to providing comprehensive care and treatment for ingrown toenails to help you get back on your feet.
DIagnosis and Treatment Options at Advanced Foot & Ankle Specialists of Arizona:

• X-rays: We use advanced imaging to evaluate underlying conditions that may be increasing the severity of the ingrown toenail.

  • Surgical Interventions: In severe or recurring cases, our experienced podiatrists offer surgical options to remove the ingrown toenail and prevent future problems.

If you're struggling with an ingrown toenail or foot pain, don’t wait—contact Advanced Foot & Ankle Specialists of Arizona today at 480-963-9000 or request an appointment online. Our team is here to help you get back to pain-free walking with effective treatments for ingrown toenails and other foot conditions.

title: What Is a Metatarsal Fracture? Symptoms and Treatment Options Explained
author: Alex M. Stewart, DPM, FACFAS
excerpt: At Advanced Foot & Ankle Specialists of Arizona, we understand how foot injuries, such as a metatarsal fracture, can significantly impact your daily life. Whether…
body: At Advanced Foot & Ankle Specialists of Arizona, we understand how foot injuries, such as a metatarsal fracture, can significantly impact your daily life. Whether you're in Chandler, Gilbert, Mesa, or Tempe, foot pain can affect your mobility, making it essential to address the issue promptly.

A metatarsal fracture is one of the most common types of foot fractures, often caused by trauma or repetitive stress. Understanding its symptoms, causes, and available treatment options can help you find relief and avoid long-term complications. In this blog, we’ll explain what a metatarsal fracture is, how it occurs, and the best ways to treat it.
What is a Metatarsal Fracture?

The metatarsals are the five long bones located in the midfoot, connecting the toes to the rest of the foot. A metatarsal fracture occurs when one of these bones is broken or cracked. This injury can range from a small hairline crack to a complete break, and it can happen to anyone, regardless of age or activity level.

Metatarsal fractures are common in athletes, especially runners, dancers, and those who engage in high-impact sports. However, they can also occur in everyday activities, such as dropping something heavy on the foot or twisting the foot awkwardly during walking or running.
Causes and Risk Factors
Metatarsal fractures can happen due to a variety of reasons, including:

• Trauma or Impact: Dropping a heavy object on the foot, a direct blow, or a sudden twisting motion can result in a fracture.

  • Repetitive Stress: Overuse injuries, such as from running, jumping, or dancing, can cause stress fractures in the metatarsals.

  • Foot Deformities: Certain foot conditions, like bunions, flat feet, or high arches, can increase the risk of fractures due to abnormal foot mechanics.

  • Improper Footwear: Wearing shoes that do not offer adequate support can increase the risk of injury, especially during physical activities.

  • Age: As people age, bones may weaken and become more prone to fractures, even from minor impacts.
Symptoms of a Metatarsal Fracture
If you have a metatarsal fracture, you may experience the following symptoms:

• Pain and tenderness in the midfoot, which may worsen with activity or pressure.

  • Swelling around the injured area.

  • Bruising or discoloration near the fracture site.

  • Difficulty walking or bearing weight on the affected foot.

  • Deformity of the foot, particularly if the fracture is severe or involves displacement of the bone.

  • Inability to move the toes or difficulty pointing or flexing them.

If you experience any of these symptoms, it’s essential to seek professional care from a podiatrist at Advanced Foot & Ankle Specialists of Arizona for an accurate diagnosis and appropriate treatment.
Diagnosing a Metatarsal Fracture

To diagnose a metatarsal fracture, Dr. Alex Stewart, DPM, FACFAS and Dr. Antonius Su, DPM will perform a physical examination to assess the location and severity of the pain. Imaging tests, such as X-rays and Ultrasound are essential to confirm the presence of a fracture and determine its type (stress fracture, hairline fracture, or complete break). In some cases, advanced imaging, like an MRI or CT scan, may be used to get a clearer view of the injury.
Treatment Options for Metatarsal Fractures
The treatment for a metatarsal fracture will depend on the type, severity, and location of the injury. Common treatment options include:
1. Conservative (Non-Surgical) Treatment
For most metatarsal fractures, especially stress fractures or minor breaks, non-surgical treatment is sufficient. This may include:

• Rest and Immobilization: Limiting movement and avoiding weight-bearing activities can promote healing. A cast, walking boot, or brace is typically used to immobilize the foot and prevent further injury.

  • Ice and Elevation: Applying ice to the injured area helps reduce swelling and pain. Elevating the foot above heart level can also alleviate swelling.

  • Pain Management: Over-the-counter pain relievers, such as ibuprofen or acetaminophen, can help manage pain and inflammation.

  • Crutches: Using crutches can help offload pressure from the injured foot, allowing the bone to heal.
2. MLS Laser Therapy

For faster healing and reduced pain, MLS Laser Therapy is an effective, non-invasive treatment. This therapy uses light energy to penetrate tissues, reduce inflammation, improve circulation, and promote the healing of bones and soft tissues. It’s a great option for patients with moderate fractures looking for enhanced recovery.
3. Surgical Treatment
In more severe cases, where the bone is displaced or the fracture is complex, surgery may be necessary to realign the bones and stabilize the foot. Surgical options include:

• Internal Fixation: Metal pins, screws, or plates may be used to hold the fractured bone in place while it heals.

  • Bone Grafting: If the fracture has caused bone loss, bone grafting may be used to stimulate healing and support the fracture site.
4. Custom Orthotics and Footwear

Once the fracture has healed, custom orthotics and properly fitting footwear are essential for preventing further injury. Custom orthotics can provide the necessary arch support and cushioning to distribute pressure evenly across the foot, helping to avoid future fractures or discomfort.
Recovery and Rehabilitation

Recovery time for a metatarsal fracture can vary based on the severity of the injury. Minor fractures may take 6-8 weeks to heal, while more complex fractures may require 8-12 weeks or longer. During recovery, physical therapy can help restore strength, flexibility, and range of motion to the foot and ankle, preventing stiffness and improving overall function.
Preventing Metatarsal Fractures
While some fractures are unavoidable, there are steps you can take to reduce the risk:

• Wear supportive footwear that provides cushioning and stability for the foot.

  • Warm-up properly before engaging in physical activities, especially high-impact sports or running.

  • Gradually increase physical activity to avoid overuse injuries and stress fractures.

  • Maintain bone health by consuming a balanced diet rich in calcium and vitamin D to promote strong bones.

If you’re experiencing foot pain, suspect a fracture, or have recently injured your foot, don’t wait to seek professional treatment. Early diagnosis and treatment can significantly reduce recovery time and prevent complications. title: Lower Extremity Wound Care: A Comprehensive Guide
author: Alex M. Stewart, DPM, FACFAS
excerpt: At Advanced Foot & Ankle Specialists of Arizona, we understand that wounds on the lower extremities can cause significant discomfort and complications, especially if…
body: At Advanced Foot & Ankle Specialists of Arizona, we understand that wounds on the lower extremities can cause significant discomfort and complications, especially if not treated properly. From diabetic foot ulcers to post-surgical recovery wounds, timely and effective care is crucial to healing and maintaining your overall foot health. As a board-certified podiatric surgeon, I, Dr. Alex Stewart, along with my colleague Dr. Antonius Su, strives to provide top-quality wound care services to patients throughout Chandler, Arizona, and surrounding cities. In this blog, we will dive into the causes, symptoms, and treatments for lower extremity wounds, with an emphasis on the advanced care options available at our practice.
What Are Lower Extremity Wounds?

Lower extremity wounds encompass a wide range of injuries or conditions affecting the feet and ankles, often including ulcers, cuts, abrasions, surgical wounds, and injuries resulting from conditions like diabetes or poor circulation. These wounds can occur due to trauma, pressure, or underlying medical conditions such as peripheral artery disease (PAD), venous insufficiency, or diabetes.
Common Types of Lower Extremity Wounds Include:

• Diabetic Foot Ulcers: Often found on the bottom of the feet, these ulcers are a common complication of diabetes. Poor blood flow and neuropathy (nerve damage) can prevent the wound from healing properly.
  • Venous Ulcers: These occur due to poor blood circulation in the legs, often affecting the lower legs near the ankles.
  • Pressure Ulcers (Bedsores): Caused by prolonged pressure on the skin, particularly for individuals who are immobile for extended periods.
  • Traumatic Injuries: Cuts, abrasions, and punctures resulting from accidents or sports injuries.
  • Post-Surgical Wounds: Wounds that develop after surgery, requiring careful management to avoid complications such as infection or delayed healing.
Causes and Risk Factors
Several factors contribute to the development of lower extremity wounds. Common causes and risk factors include:

• Diabetes: High blood sugar levels can impair circulation and delay wound healing.
  • Poor Circulation: Conditions like PAD or venous insufficiency can reduce blood flow to the feet, slowing down the healing process.
  • Trauma or Injury: Accidents, falls, or overuse can lead to open wounds or abrasions.
  • Infection: An untreated injury can lead to infection, which complicates the healing process.
  • Immobilization: Prolonged periods of immobility, such as being bedridden, can cause pressure ulcers or sores.
Symptoms of Lower Extremity Wounds
Symptoms may vary depending on the type and severity of the wound, but common signs include:

• Pain or tenderness at the wound site
  • Redness, swelling, or warmth around the wound
  • Discharge or pus, which may indicate infection
  • Difficulty walking or moving due to pain or discomfort
  • Unpleasant odor or changes in the wound appearance, signaling infection or complications
Treatment Options for Lower Extremity Wounds

Proper treatment of lower extremity wounds is essential to prevent infection, promote healing, and avoid complications like amputation. At Advanced Foot & Ankle Specialists of Arizona, we offer a variety of advanced treatment options tailored to meet your needs.

Our wound care team follows a structured protocol to assess, clean/debride, and dress the wound, ensuring it is properly protected from infection. We use specialized dressings designed to create the optimal environment for healing.

Proper footwear and support are essential for preventing pressure ulcers and further injury. Custom orthotics are designed to redistribute weight and reduce friction, while appropriate shoes protect the foot from injury and promote better healing.

In cases of deeper wounds, our practice uses advanced diagnostic tools like X-rays and ultrasound to assess the extent of damage, detect any foreign bodies, and rule out bone infection (osteomyelitis).

In more severe cases, or when a wound doesn’t heal with conservative measures, surgical intervention may be necessary. This could involve debridement (removal of dead tissue), skin grafting, or other procedures to close the wound and promote healing.
Preventive Foot Care Tips for Lower Extremity Wounds
Preventing lower extremity wounds is crucial, especially for individuals with conditions like diabetes or poor circulation. Here are some tips to help maintain foot health:

• Check Your Feet Daily: Inspect your feet regularly for cuts, blisters, or other signs of injury, especially if you have diabetes.
  • Wear Proper Footwear: Choose shoes that fit well and provide adequate support to reduce friction and pressure.
  • Stay Active: Regular exercise can improve circulation and reduce the risk of conditions that contribute to poor healing.
  • Keep Skin Moisturized: Dry, cracked skin is more prone to injury, so keep your feet well-moisturized.
  • Seek Professional Care: If you notice any unusual symptoms, such as redness, swelling, or pain in your feet, consult a podiatrist immediately.

If you’re experiencing a wound on your foot or ankle, don’t wait—early treatment is key to preventing complications and promoting healing. Contact Advanced Foot & Ankle Specialists of Arizona today at (480) 963-9000 or book an appointment online to receive comprehensive, compassionate care tailored to your needs. We’re here to help you put your best foot forward again.

title: Is Platelet-Rich Plasma the Right Treatment for Me?
author: Alex M. Stewart, DPM, FACFAS
excerpt: Are you experiencing persistent foot or ankle pain that doesn’t seem to improve with traditional treatments? If so, you may be wondering about newer, more advanced…
body: Are you experiencing persistent foot or ankle pain that doesn’t seem to improve with traditional treatments? If so, you may be wondering about newer, more advanced therapies that could offer relief. One such treatment is Platelet-Rich Plasma (PRP) therapy, which has gained significant attention in the medical community for its ability to accelerate healing and reduce pain in soft tissue injuries. At Advanced Foot & Ankle Specialists of Arizona, we offer PRP therapy as part of our comprehensive approach to treating common foot and ankle conditions.

In this blog, we’ll explore whether PRP is the right treatment option for you, how it works, and the conditions it can help treat. We’ll also discuss the potential benefits and risks of this innovative therapy, helping you make an informed decision about your care.
What is Platelet-Rich Plasma (PRP) Therapy?

Platelet-Rich Plasma (PRP) is a regenerative medicine technique that uses a patient’s own blood to stimulate healing. Blood contains various components, including platelets, which play a crucial role in tissue repair. In PRP therapy, blood is drawn from the patient, processed to concentrate the platelets, and then injected into the area of injury or inflammation. The high concentration of platelets promotes healing by releasing growth factors that stimulate tissue regeneration and reduce inflammation.
What Conditions Can PRP Help Treat?

PRP therapy is particularly effective for treating conditions that involve soft tissue injuries, chronic inflammation, and degeneration. At Advanced Foot & Ankle Specialists of Arizona, we use PRP to treat a variety of foot and ankle conditions, including:

• Plantar Fasciitis: This common condition causes pain in the bottom of the heel and is often the result of inflammation in the plantar fascia. PRP can help reduce inflammation and promote healing of this tissue.
  • Achilles Tendonitis: Chronic inflammation of the Achilles tendon can cause significant pain, especially in athletes. PRP injections can accelerate the healing of the tendon and reduce pain.
  • Ankle Sprains: For patients with chronic or severe ankle sprains, PRP can speed up recovery and reduce pain associated with ligament damage.
  • Tendinitis: PRP is effective for treating tendinitis in the foot and ankle, including conditions like peroneal tendonitis and posterior tibial tendonitis.
  • Arthritis: While not a cure, PRP can provide significant relief for arthritis in the foot and ankle by reducing inflammation and promoting cartilage repair.
How Does PRP Work?
The process of PRP therapy involves several key steps:

1. Blood Draw: A small amount of blood is drawn from the patient, typically from the arm.
  2. Blood Processing: The blood is placed in a centrifuge, which separates the red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. The platelets are concentrated in a small amount of plasma.
  3. Injection: The concentrated PRP is injected directly into the injured or inflamed area of the foot or ankle.

Since PRP uses the patient’s own blood, the risk of allergic reactions or rejection is minimal. The concentrated platelets release growth factors that encourage healing, reduce pain, and promote tissue regeneration.
Benefits of PRP Therapy
There are several benefits of PRP therapy that make it an attractive treatment option for patients dealing with chronic foot and ankle conditions:

• Natural Healing: Since PRP uses your body’s own cells, the treatment is natural and has fewer risks than synthetic drugs or treatments.
  • Minimally Invasive: PRP therapy is a non-surgical procedure, meaning there’s no need for incisions or long recovery times.
  • Reduced Pain and Inflammation: PRP can significantly reduce pain and inflammation in injured or inflamed areas, allowing for better mobility and function.
  • Faster Recovery: By stimulating tissue regeneration, PRP therapy can accelerate the healing process and get you back to your daily activities faster.
  • Low Risk of Side Effects: As a procedure that uses your own blood, the risk of side effects is minimal, and complications are rare.
Is PRP Right for You?

PRP therapy is a promising treatment, but it’s not right for everyone. To determine if PRP is the best option for you, a comprehensive evaluation by a podiatric expert is essential. At Advanced Foot & Ankle Specialists of Arizona, Dr. Alex Stewart, DPM, FACFAS and Dr. Antonius Su, DPM will evaluate your condition, medical history, and treatment goals to determine whether PRP therapy is appropriate.
PRP may be recommended if:

• You have a chronic foot or ankle injury that hasn’t responded well to conservative treatments such as rest, physical therapy, or medications.
  • You are looking for a non-surgical solution to reduce pain and improve healing.
  • You are in good overall health and can tolerate a blood draw and injection.

However, PRP may not be suitable if you have certain health conditions, such as blood disorders, active infections, or if you are taking medications that interfere with platelet function. Your doctor will discuss these factors with you during the consultation.
What to Expect During PRP Treatment

The procedure is typically performed in-office and takes about 30 to 60 minutes. After the blood is drawn and processed, the PRP will be injected into the affected area. The injection may cause some temporary discomfort or mild swelling, but most patients can resume normal activities within a day or two.

You may experience some soreness at the injection site for a few days, and it may take several weeks to notice the full benefits of the treatment as the body heals. In some cases, multiple PRP injections may be required to achieve optimal results.blo

title: Do You Have Heel Pain? Recognize the Early Signs of Plantar Fasciitis
author: Alex M. Stewart, DPM, FACFAS
excerpt: If you’ve been experiencing heel pain, especially after getting out of bed in the morning or after prolonged periods of sitting, you may be dealing with a common foot…
body: If you’ve been experiencing heel pain, especially after getting out of bed in the morning or after prolonged periods of sitting, you may be dealing with a common foot condition known as plantar fasciitis. At Advanced Foot & Ankle Specialists of Arizona, we see many patients in Chandler, Mesa, Gilbert, and Tempe who suffer from this painful condition. In this blog, we’ll walk you through the early signs of plantar fasciitis, its causes, and the treatment options available to get you back on your feet.
What is Plantar Fasciitis?

Plantar fasciitis is an inflammation of the plantar fascia, a thick band of tissue that runs across the bottom of your foot, connecting your heel bone to your toes. This condition is one of the most common causes of heel pain, and it typically presents itself as pain in the bottom of the heel, especially first thing in the morning.
Symptoms of Plantar Fasciitis
Recognizing the early signs of plantar fasciitis is key to receiving prompt treatment and avoiding further discomfort. The most common symptoms include:

• Heel pain: A sharp, stabbing pain on the bottom of the heel, usually worse with your first steps in the morning or after periods of inactivity.
  • Pain after long periods of sitting: After sitting for a while, standing up can cause pain and stiffness in the heel.
  • Tenderness and swelling: Swelling around the heel or arch, which may worsen throughout the day with prolonged walking or standing.
  • Tightness in the foot: A feeling of tightness in the foot, especially in the arch or near the heel, when walking or stretching.
If you experience any of these symptoms, it's important to seek treatment early to avoid the pain becoming more severe and chronic.
Causes and Risk Factors of Plantar Fasciitis
Plantar fasciitis is most often caused by excessive stress and strain on the plantar fascia. There are several factors that increase the risk of developing this condition:

1. Overuse: People who are on their feet for long periods of time, such as athletes, teachers, or factory workers, are more likely to develop plantar fasciitis.
  2. Improper footwear: Shoes with insufficient arch support, cushioning, or an improper fit can contribute to plantar fascia strain.
  3. Tight calf muscles: Tightness in the calf muscles can lead to added stress on the plantar fascia, which can contribute to inflammation.
  4. Obesity: Carrying extra weight puts more strain on your feet, increasing the likelihood of developing plantar fasciitis.
  5. Age: Plantar fasciitis is most common in people between the ages of 40 and 60.
  6. Flat feet or high arches: Abnormal foot mechanics, such as flat feet or high arches, can alter the way weight is distributed when walking, leading to increased strain on the plantar fascia.
Treatment Options for Plantar Fasciitis

If you're suffering from heel pain, you don't have to endure it. At Advanced Foot & Ankle Specialists of Arizona, we offer a range of effective treatments designed to reduce pain, promote healing, and prevent the condition from worsening.
1. Physical Therapy and Stretching

Physical therapy is one of the most effective ways to treat plantar fasciitis. Stretching exercises designed to loosen the calf muscles and plantar fascia can help alleviate pain and improve flexibility. Our team will provide you with a tailored exercise plan to improve the strength and flexibility of your foot.
2. Custom Orthotics

Custom orthotics are specially designed shoe inserts that help correct abnormal foot mechanics and relieve pressure on the plantar fascia. At our practice, we provide custom-made orthotics that support the arch and heel, offering long-term relief and helping prevent recurrence of the condition.
3. MLS Laser Therapy

One of the innovative treatments available at our clinic is MLS Laser Therapy. This non-invasive therapy uses laser energy to reduce inflammation, accelerate healing, and provide pain relief for patients suffering from plantar fasciitis. MLS Laser Therapy promotes tissue repair and stimulates circulation, making it an excellent treatment option for chronic heel pain.
4. X-ray and Ultrasound Imaging

If your plantar fasciitis symptoms are persistent or severe, we may recommend an X-ray or ultrasound to assess the extent of the damage. Imaging can help rule out other conditions such as fractures or stress injuries and ensure that we develop the most effective treatment plan for you.
5. Corticosteroid Injections

For patients who experience severe pain, corticosteroid injections can provide temporary relief by reducing inflammation in the affected area. These injections are typically used in conjunction with other treatment methods.
1. Platelet Rich Plasma Injections

Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) works by using a concentration of platelets derived from a person's own blood to promote healing. The platelets contain growth factors that stimulate tissue repair and reduce inflammation when injected into an injured area, enhancing the body's natural healing processes.
7. Foot and Ankle Taping

Taping techniques can provide support to the foot, reduce strain on the plantar fascia, and help alleviate pain. Our team can demonstrate how to tape your foot properly to provide relief and enhance healing.
8. Surgery (in severe cases)

If conservative treatments don’t provide relief after 6 to 12 months, surgical intervention may be considered. This is usually reserved for severe cases where there is significant damage to the plantar fascia or if other treatments have failed.
Prevention Tips for Plantar Fasciitis
While some factors are beyond your control, there are several steps you can take to reduce the risk of developing plantar fasciitis or prevent it from returning:

• Wear proper footwear: Choose shoes with good arch support, cushioning, and a wide toe box. Avoid wearing high heels or shoes with inadequate support.
  • Stretch regularly: Stretching your calves and feet can help prevent tightness and reduce strain on the plantar fascia.
  • Maintain a healthy weight: Reducing excess weight can reduce pressure on your feet, helping to prevent or alleviate heel pain.
  • Avoid overuse: Gradually increase your activity level to prevent overuse and injury to the plantar fascia.
